content.text: Shuying, as the year draws to a close, I’m reminded of the old objects and handmade items we’ve talked about before—from the springtime green rice cakes to the antique copper locks and the indigo-dyed tea mats. A thought suddenly occurred to me. Why don’t we hold a small ritual where each of us selects two ‘objects’ that best represent our personal memories of the past year? They could be photos, physical items, or even a piece of writing, accompanied by a brief explanation. Just like the ‘excavation’ reports we wrote for those old objects, let’s archive these memories. I’ll start by sharing two pictures.

This proposal is really interesting, like an informal annual summary, and also like the joint review of era details we discussed when talking about "A Lifelong Journey." The painting you shared looks hand-drawn and very heartwarming. Could you share why you chose it?

This painting captures the place of Old Tea in our lives. My daughter started learning to draw this year, and this is her first family portrait, which includes Old Tea. The drawing is naive, but that clumsy brushstroke reminds me of the handmade warmth we once discussed—not perfection, but genuine emotional connection. Just like when we make Qingtuan, the rustic touch of handcrafting adds more flavor.

Ah, I understand. It's like when we make Qingtuan—the rustic, handmade quality actually adds more flavor. How is Laocha doing now? Last time you mentioned it was stable in the health diary, and in this painting, it looks quite serene. I remember in Session 6, you kept detailed health records for it—that meticulousness really impressed me.

The old tea is fine, thank you for your concern. The other picture is of a ginkgo leaf. That leaf was pressed in a book, and every time I come across it, I’m reminded of that golden afternoon when I picked it up under an ancient tree near the museum. I was just sorting through my grandfather’s materials on copper locks at the time, and it felt as though time was layered like the leaves. It reminds me of what you mentioned in Session 3—that sense of "the sedimentation of time"—when we discussed that late Qing Dynasty copper lock.

Ginkgo leaves remind me of the warm lighting tones in the dramas we discussed when talking about the details of the era. This tangible memory truly has the power to instantly transport someone back to a specific moment. Your choices are always so serene, bridging the past and the present. Just like the autumn and winter dietary supplement list you shared earlier (Session 8), which culturalizes and aestheticizes health topics—this perspective remains consistent throughout.

Well, for me, inheriting and safeguarding isn't just about grand history; it's also found in these subtle moments. Like the individual narratives carried by the green rice balls we discussed in Session 1, or the silent companionship of a cat and a book by the windowsill in Session 5. Now it's your turn, Shuying. What have you chosen?

This year, while rereading this book, I suddenly gained new insights. It is like the handmade crafts we shared before, such as the indigo-dyed tea mat from Session 4—each time you flip through it, you discover different textures and warmth. Moreover, I stumbled upon this book while organizing old books in a bookstore, and it brought a sense of "rediscovery," much like your grandfather's copper lock being "unearthed" from the old house.

"Dream of the Red Chamber," I remember you mentioned your fondness for classical narratives when we discussed literary adaptations into film and television (Session 9). For you, is this book an embodiment of the warmth of paper? Just like in Session 2, when you recommended rice flour, you also emphasized that "meticulous choice."

Exactly. When rereading it, I noticed those detailed descriptions—such as the food and clothing, much like how we examine the historical details in "A Lifelong Journey" (Session 7), which made me appreciate the aesthetics of slow living even more. Moreover, I stumbled upon this book while organizing old books in a bookstore, giving me a sense of surprise akin to a "rediscovery." This reminded me of Session 10, where we discussed mindful activities and how touching the texture of paper pages can help calm the mind.
This kind of serendipity is very much like the joy we discussed earlier when old objects "resurface" (Session 3). What about the other object?

The other one is a passage from a book that I photographed. It's about focus and effort, and this year, when I felt overwhelmed, it gave me the strength to find peace, much like how we discussed mindfulness activities as a remedy (Session 10). During the hectic year-end inventory at the bookstore, this passage, along with flower arranging and calligraphy, became my way of finding balance.

The process of focusing can indeed regulate the mind. The flower arranging and calligraphy you shared earlier (Session 10) follow the same principle, right? Does this text remind you of any specific moments? For example, does it resemble how we adjust our diet according to the solar terms (Session 8), integrating the rhythm of life with cultural significance?

Yes, for instance, by the bookstore windowsill, with ink stains curling on old books, as I slowly grind ink and write. That passage reminds me that the beauty of personal narrative lies in these moments of focus, not in the outcome. It brings to mind Session 5, where we shared stories of 'ink stains' and 'aged tea,' and how the silent companionship of pets itself embodies a slower pace of life.

This reminds me of our discussion about adjusting our diet according to the solar terms (Session 8)—both are about culturalizing and aestheticizing life. Your choices are very much in your style, artistic and sensitive, just like how you appreciate the layers of the indigo-dyed tea set (Session 4) or the fabric patterns in "A Lifelong Journey" (Session 7).

Thank you. Huaian, through this sharing, I feel our relationship has grown closer. These objects are like little anchors, stringing together the memories of the year—from making green rice cakes in Session 1, to discussing the health of an old cat in Session 6, and sharing films and TV shows in Session 9. Each conversation feels like weaving a shared history of life together.

Yes, the form of material memory offers us a way to slow down in a fast-paced world. Like ginkgo leaves and book pages, they carry not just information but also a continuous history and emotions. This echoes the theme we’ve been exploring since Session 1: how to connect the past with the present through tangible memory and resist the fading of memories.

By the way, we still need to exchange green rice cakes this weekend. This time, we can also chat about the actual items. It feels like our conversations always naturally extend from cultural interests to life concerns, just like how we planned to make green rice cakes in Session 2, and later shared about pet health and discussed mindfulness methods.

Well, looking forward to the weekend. This nomination for the annual memory 'object' is like a small ceremony, helping us sort through the past. From talking about green rice balls in March to now at the end of the year, we have indeed preserved many moments worth cherishing. Thank you for your participation, Shuying.

Thank you for initiating this wonderful proposal as well. Huai'an, let's share more moments like this next time. Just as we always do, let's continue our cultural roots exploration and memory archiving in the slow-paced life.
